MODAL INTERCHANGE

Modat interchange is the temporary convergence of two parallel, major and minor key centers, in a single progression. Not to be confused with relative keys, which share the same nates and key signatures, parallef major and minor keys have different notes and harmonies, but share the same fonic. For example, C major is parallel to C minor: F minor is parallel to F major: and sO on. .

Modal interchange

To understand modal interchange, we need to compare the differences and similarities between major and minor scale harmony. In Fig. 13A, the top row of chords represents the harmonized triads In the key of C major. Below them are the triads from the parallel key of C minor. The only similarities ara that the roots of the |, li, IV, and V chords are the same. Everything else is different: the chord qualities, and the root placement of the chords built off the 3rd, 6th, and 7th degrees.
